To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
CGI-I and CGI-dif have a similar validity in depicting change and that the CGI ratings of patients, therapists and the team do not fully agree.

(1) CGI-I and CGI-SDiff are not interchangeable measures of clinical change; (2) CGI-I is more sensitive to change and is therefore recommended for clinical change assessment; and (3) there are substantial discrepancies between patient and clinician ratings of depression severity, and these are not explained by the use of the CGI.

the validity of the Clinical Global Impres-sion Scale, which has become one of psychiatry's most widely used assessment tools.
the CGI's validity and the influence of the perspective from which it is rated.

the question whether the CGI is an adequate tool for assessing the severity of psychiatric conditions and the degree of improvement in psychotherapeutic settings and, if so, which of its subscales is most appropriate for that purpose.

CGI is a valid measure for the evaluation of treatment effects in clinical trials but should be used with caution in clinical practice.

the CGI-I seems to be a more valid measure of clinical improvement, while the CGI-S dif is a less valid measure of clinical severity.
